Does there exist $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with lower density $>1/3$ such that $a+b\neq 2^k$ for any $a,b\in A$ and $k\geq 0$?
#1136: [Mu11]
number theory
A question asked by Erdős at the DMV conference in Berlin 1987 (as reported in [Mu11]). Achieving density $1/3$ is trivial, taking $A$ to be all multiples of $3$.
Müller [Mu11] settled this question in the affirmative: in fact one can take $A$ to be the set of all integers congruent to $3\cdot 2^i\pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for any $i\geq 0$, which has density $1/2$. Müller also proved this is best possible, in that $A$ with the property in the question has lower density at most $1/2$.

 Remarkably, the greedy sequence provides the exact same solution. 
To elaborate on this, on the one hand we define $A$ as the set of all positive integers congruent to $3 \cdot 2^i \pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for some $i \ge 0$. Equivalently, $A$ is the set of all positive integers whose largest odd divisor is congruent to $3 \pmod{4}$. On the other hand, inductively define $b_j$ as the smallest (unused) positive integer such that $b_i + b_j \neq 2^k$ for all $1 \le i \le j$ and all $k \ge 0$, and set $B = \{b_1, b_2, \ldots\}$. 
Then it is clear that $A$ has density $1/4 + 1/8 + \cdots = 1/2$, while it is also clear that $B$ has the property that $B+B$ avoids powers of two.
What is less clear however (it was at least a nice surprise to me when I just realized this) is that $A$ and $B$ are equal to one another!
Indeed, assume by induction that $A \cap [1, 2^k] = B \cap [1, 2^k]$, which is certainly true for $k = 0$. Then an integer $n$ with $2^k < n < 2^{k+1}$ is in $B$ precisely when $a := 2^{k+1} - n$ is not in $B$. By the induction hypothesis this happens precisely when we can write $a = 2^l \cdot (4m+1)$ for some $l \le k-1$. But this means we can write $$n = 2^{k+1} - 2^l \cdot (4m+1) = 2^l \cdot (2^{k+1-l} - (4m+1)) = 2^l \cdot (4m'+3) \in A.$$As every step of this argument is reversible, we get $A \cap [1, 2^{k+1}] = B \cap [1, 2^{k+1}]$, and hence $A = B$.

 Some sundry remarks:
1) A nice related theorem that I found in Nathanson's book Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets is that if $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ satisfies $|A| > \frac{n}{3}$, then some power of two can be written as the sum of at most $4$ elements of $A$. Lev was the first to show this, and they later extended their result to $5$ distinct elements.
2) I have asked Aristotle to slightly upgrade Lorenzo's formalization to prove both that natural density of $\frac{1}{2}$ is possible, as well as the fact that any set $A$ for which $a+b \neq 2^k$ for all $a,b \in A$ has upper density at most $\frac{1}{2}$. You can check it here, and note that the upper bound is slightly stronger than what is stated in the remarks, which only mention lower density.
3) In fact, an even stronger and more general upper bound result is true that I can't help but share (and whose proof can be found at the end of this comment);
Theorem.
Let $S = \{s_1 < s_2 < \cdots \} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be any infinite set of positive integers for which 
\begin{equation*} 
s_{k+1} \le 2s_k + 2 \qquad \qquad (1)
\end{equation*}holds for all $k$. Then for any positive integer $n$ and any set $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ satisfying 
\begin{equation*}
|A| > \frac{n + s_1}{2} \qquad \qquad (2)
\end{equation*}we have $(A+A) \cap S \neq \emptyset$. 
4) The previous theorem implies in particular the neat result that for any $S = \{s_1 < s_2 < \cdots \} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfying $s_{k+1} \le 2s_k + 2$ and any $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with upper density larger than $\frac{1}{2}$, we have that $A+A$ contains infinitely many elements of $S$. 
5) The results mentioned at 3) and 4) are also proven in the formalization I linked, and note that these results include the powers of two as a special case.
6) Finally, here is the promised proof:
Proof.
If $n \le s_1$, then the right-hand side of equation $(2)$ is at least $n$, so the statement is vacuous. Hence, let $n > s_1$ and assume by induction that the theorem is true for all positive integers smaller than $n$. We then define $k$ to be such that $s_k \le n < s_{k+1}$, and let $m$ be such that $n+m = s_{k+1}$. 
First, if $m = 1$, then using equation $(2)$ we get $$|A| > \frac{n + s_1}{2} \ge \frac{n + 1}{2} = \frac{s_{k+1}}{2},$$so that $A$ contains $\{j, s_{k+1} - j\}$ for some $1 \le j \le \frac{s_{k+1}}{2}$ by the pigeonhole principle. Similarly, if $n = s_k$, then $$|A| > \frac{n + s_1}{2} > \frac{s_{k}}{2}$$in which case $A$ contains $\{j, s_{k} - j\}$ for some $1 \le j \le \frac{s_{k}}{2}$. We may therefore assume both $m \ge 2$ and $n \ge s_k+1$.
Now, combining these latter two inequalities with equation $(1)$, we obtain $$2 \le m = s_{k+1} - n \le s_{k+1} - s_k - 1 \le s_k+1 \le n.$$In particular, we may apply the induction hypothesis to $m-1$. That is, if 
\begin{equation*}
|A \cap \{1, 2, \ldots, m-1\}| > \frac{m-1+s_1}{2}, \qquad (3)
\end{equation*}then we are done by induction. We may therefore assume that the cardinality on the left-hand side of equation $(3)$ is smaller than or equal to $\frac{m-1+s_1}{2}$, which implies by equation $(2)$ that
\begin{align*}
|A \cap \{m, m+1, \ldots, n\}| &\ge \frac{n-m+2}{2} \\
&=\frac{s_{k+1}- 2m + 2}{2} \\
&= \frac{s_{k+1}}{2} - m + 1.
\end{align*}Hence, by one final application of the pigeonhole principle we deduce that $A$ contains $\{j, s_{k+1} - j\}$ for some $m \le j \le \frac{s_{k+1}}{2}$, finishing the proof.
